title: Boxing: stance, punches, defense, and rules
note: Boxing uses four punches: jab, cross, hook, and uppercut. Power comes from the legs and hip rotation, not the arm alone. Footwork keeps the base under you, and defense moves the head or deflects the glove. Bouts are scored round by round on the ten-point must system.

read.title: Why the jab comes first
text: Boxing has only four punches, yet it is endlessly varied. The jab is a straight punch with the lead hand; the cross, a straight punch with the rear hand; the hook, a short curved punch from the side; the uppercut, a rising punch from below. Orthodox boxers lead with the left side, southpaws with the right.

Coaches teach the jab first because it does so many jobs. It is the closest weapon to the target, so it measures distance, disturbs the opponent's view, and opens the way for the cross. The cross carries more power because the rear foot pushes and the rear hip turns, sending the weight of the body through the fist.

Footwork protects that power. Boxers step first with the foot nearest the direction they want to go and avoid crossing their feet, so the base stays wide enough to punch and absorb punches. Defense uses the same economy: a slip moves the head off a straight punch, a roll dips under a hook, and a parry turns a punch aside with a small touch.
Judges score each round separately on the ten-point must system, rewarding clean punches, control of the pace and space, and competitiveness.
